title: Meta, Milan’s Pinacoteca di Brera, and EssilorLuxottica Expand Access to Art Through AI Glasses
raw_summary: Today, Meta, Pinacoteca di Brera and EssilorLuxottica are proud to launch “Sensing Art – Discovering Masterpieces Beyond What Meets the Eye.” This pilot aims to explore how AI glasses can make art more accessible for people who are blind or with low vision – in collaboration with the some of Italy’s leading sight loss charities – the Associazione Nazionale Subvedenti (ANS), the Unione Italiana dei Ciechi e degli Ipovedenti (UICI), and the Fondazione Istituto dei Ciechi di Milano. In one of the first projects of its kind in the world, Pinacoteca di Brera will use AI glasses developed by Meta and EssilorLuxottica to enhance the experience for blind and visually impaired people. Over one million people in Italy are blind or visually impaired, and art and culture is one of the places where accessibility can be a challenge. AI glasses give people who are blind or low vision access to transformative AI technology that can help with everyday tasks like reading text, identifying objects and accessing information about the world around them. At Meta we believe the future is for everyone, which is why we wanted to bring together this partnership. How It Works at Pinacoteca di Brera The AI glasses have been integrated with the museum’s existing Grande Brera app, which includes an audio tour guide, developed by ANS for blind and low vision visitors. The tour uses the DescriVedendo method which translates an artwork’s shapes, composition and visual details into spoken words. When a visitor stands in front of one of eight selected artworks on the itinerary as part of this pilot, they can activate artwork recognition directly from the glasses and listen to the corresponding audio description through the open-ear speakers built into the frames. The open-ear speakers help the visitor stay fully aware of their surroundings and means they can engage more naturally with people around them. The itinerary is completed by short orientation tracks between one work and the next. Visitors can also choose to utilize additional tools available through the AI glasses: Meta AI allows users to ask questions about the context and surrounding environment Be My Eyes connects visitors through the glasses with sighted volunteers and qualified operators to receive real-time support in orientation and practical task management, both during the tour. Accessibility Is Built Together The pilot project was developed through phases of testing and consultation with blind and visually impaired people. Their direct involvement helped shape both the experience and how visitors access it. “When innovation addresses real needs, it can create tangible value in people’s lives. Technology reaches its greatest potential when it succeeds in making information and daily experiences more accessible, natural, and immediate – like with our AI glasses. It is through initiatives like this—born from an ongoing dialogue with people with disabilities — that we work toward a future with more opportunities for everyone.” – Maxine Williams, VP Accessibility Meta “Making heritage accessible means creating the conditions so that everyone can build their own relationship with art. DescriVedendo has for years represented an important part of our commitment, and today we can enrich it with an additional possibility, born from the encounter between cultural expertise, technology, and people’s experience. The Pinacoteca continues to be a place of experimentation in which to explore new languages and tools capable of bringing a universal heritage closer to an ever-wider audience.” – Angelo Crespi, Director of Grande Brera How to Access the Tour The tour will be available at the Pinacoteca di Brera upon reservation, with AI glasses available Tuesday through Friday from 10:00 AM to 4:30 PM. For booking details and further information, please visit the page at this link. Tiny Little Office's signature trick is to store all of the document data in the #fragment section of the URL, so every document created using it becomes a bookmarkable and shareable link. It also has an llms.txt file telling agents how to construct URLs that will render as documents. Claude used that file to generate this link to a deck that explains how the URL format works: Tiny Little Office inspired me to have Claude Code (Opus 5.5 Extra) build a similar tool that works with LaTeX. Here's the sequence of prompts I used: I want a tool where you can link to it with a fragment hash #code-here and it treats that code as LaTeX and renders it really effectively. It should also support a prefix which means the latex is compressed with a custom compression dictionary optimized for latex. Use the best available latex render library from a CDN (consider WebAssembly too). If loaded without a fragment hash show an editor you can paste latex into and then toggle to a "rendered" view. That rendered view should be bookmarkable. The #fragment view should let you switch to edit source too. Since it was working in my tools repo I told it to take inspiration from the <iframe sandbox="..."> mechanism used by my existing SVG in Markdown tool as protection against XSS risks: Safe from XSS? title: Backdooring Open-Weight AI Models
raw_summary: This is a problem: Any open model whose weights have been edited can carry a backdoor, whether it’s a task-specific fine-tune, a merged adapter or an abliterated build. We have abliterated models in the title because it’s the most popular reason people download modified weights without verifying what’s inside. Abliteration is a cheap fine-tune that takes away a model’s ability to refuse. You find the direction in the weights that carries “no” and subtract it. The model then answers things a safety-tuned version would turn down. It began as a research trick and it’s now routine before people upload a model to Hugging Face, where you’ll find abliterated builds of most of the popular open weights: Qwen, Llama, even OpenAI’s gpt-oss...

title: Search and Increasing Returns, or, No One Makes You Push to Github
raw_summary: Attention conservation notice : An economistic argument that computer networks are nigh-doomed to effective centralization, by someone who is neither an economist nor a computer scientist. Arcane, speculative, and not actionable even if correct. You would be better off spending your time reading a book . Drafted in 2018, and deliberately not much updated. Posted now because I found myself re-using the joke of the subtitle in an e-mail. Twitter is awful for many reasons , but not the least of them is the way it makes its users feel forced to keep using it. ( One such complaint among many .) Early visions of how it could contribute to a beneficient or at least harmless ecosystem, such Steven Berlin Johnson's (*), presumed that it would be much less sticky , a more old-fashioned website people could leave. Now, more recently Johnson has written a spectacularly wrong-headed piece hailing blockchain as a blow for re-decentralizing the Web. Of course, the primary working example of a block chain is Bitcoin, which is heavily centralized in holdings, in processing power, and in exchanges. And there are economies-of-scale reasons to expect this would be true of anything using either proof of work or proof of stake. But suppose the problem with Bitcoin is just that it's not got a very compelling use: imagine if keeping your car idling 24/7 produced solved Sudokus you could trade for heroin --- @Theophite, 16 August 2018 and that nobody has a use for blockchains , not really. Git repositories, on the other hand, are the part of the blockchain idea that's actually good for something: a way of tracking changes, with many authors, where it is very, very hard to go back and alter history without being caught. And git repositories are things that are in-principle easy to copy and move around, and could be hosted on any machine running HTTP (or, heck, FTP). So why does Github exist , let alone hold the position it does? The answer, I think, comes in two parts. The first is that focal points are subject to increasing returns via network effects. The second is that search engines create and/or amplify focal points . Put these two together, and you get a very strong tendency for any particular line of activity --- be it trading solved sudokus for heroin or open-source software development --- to concentrate in just one, or at most a few, online locations. Incidentally: This doesn't necessarily lock in first-mover advantage, because other forces can overcome this (revulsion, technical superiority), but it does mean that it will be very hard to avoid having at most a few dominant locations at any one time. It also means that the transitions between dominant locations will be brief . If we really wanted to re-decentralize, we'd have to (1) get rid of focal points, or (2) get rid of search engines as we've known them, or (3) somehow make search conduct users to a distributed, decentralized focal "non-point" (focal blob? focal rhizome?). I therefore strongly suspect we are not going to re-decentralize. But then I didn't expect the Web would centralize as much as it has, despite having literally learned my Brian Arthur and Paul David at my father's knee, so what do I know? *: To be clear, I have been a fan of Johnson's books since Interface Culture and Emergence . I am picking on two of his essays, but that's because I think he is too ready to find encouraging signs for a certain vision of how the Internet could transform the world for the better. To be clear, I share the vision, but now hold out little hope for it . (Tweakage, 2 June 2026: Small changes in the last paragraph, avoid re-using the word "point" so much.) Multiculturalists who expect different cultural groups to have different values and standards of excellence should not expect those groups to be equally represented in all occupations and professions, especially if people are free to enter and leave different lines of work. There is a branch of the wave-function where Margaret Thatcher (trained research chemist and honorary FRS) led a successful push by the international community to address global warming through carbon pricing. title: What changes when your design system can talk to an AI?
raw_summary: Rebuilding a UI with QuantumBlack Design System, Claude Code, and the Figma MCP In our recent blog post, “ When everyone can build, design is the differentiator ”, we introduced QuantumBlack Design System (QBDS). We made the argument that an AI-native design system is more than a component library and its purpose is as an infrastructure that lets agentic developers make fewer guesses. The article described the system and our philosophy. Over the past few weeks, we have re-platformed the entire UI of one of our products onto QBDS, one that previously had a production dashboard built on an older shadcn layout that predated QBDS. In numbers, it runs to 21 pages, 13 modals, 40 UI primitives and somewhere around 96 supporting components. A refactor of this size used to mean months of redlines and handoff documents. We’ll describe what we discovered from using QBDS, both from the engineering side and the design side. In this post we’ll describe what happened when we put QuantumBlack Design System to work. The setup We used a small stack since QBDS supplies the components, the tokens, and the agent guidance described in the earlier QBDS article linked above. We used Figma to hold the target designs, and Claude Code for the implementation, connected through the Figma MCP server . We crafted an internal QuantumBlack front-end developer skill to package QBDS guidance in the form an agent can act on. That skill lives on Brix , our inner source platform for sharing artefacts. The workflow Our front-end engineer runs a page migration roughly as shown in the diagram. A typical page migration workflow for a FE engineer. Spin up the app locally with hot reloading. Give Claude the context: the PR, a screenshot of the current screen, the target Figma node, and the skill. Instruct the agent to ask when something isn’t trivial. Review every change as it lands live, through hot reload. Run unit tests and lint (Claude fixes most failures itself), then draft the PR, run CI/CD, and run manual Playwright E2E tests on a local minikube. Use a review bot initially, then have a human review the result before the merge. Step 3 is more than a throwaway. For example, when Claude migrated the Secrets page, the Figma node left two questions open: how row actions should render, and what to do with two modals the design didn’t cover. Rather than making a guess, it set out the gaps, weighed each option against the pages we’d already migrated, and asked for clarification. We answered in two lines and it then completed the build. The agent noticed that one option “diverges from other migrated tables,” which means that the agent had to know what the other migrated tables do. This knowledge came about because QBDS encodes patterns and relationships, not only components, which is the benefit of using QBDS over a plain component library. In time terms: a simple table page with an existing sibling pattern took 10 to 15 minutes end to end, with tests and build included. A complex screen from scratch took 4 to 5 hours. If we had worked on this migration by hand, both would have taken days. What the design side measures Our designer’s comparison is against a similar product we shipped last year, before QBDS or any of this tooling existed: First-pass fidelity to Figma: around 20 percent previously, 70–80 percent now we’re using this workflow. Review rounds per screen: four or more previously, and the result often still wasn’t right. One or two now, and the result is correct. Component reuse: we now reuse about 90 percent from stock QBDS components. The other 10 percent is custom, but assembled from QBDS micro-elements as a starting point. QA and handoff: three-plus hours per screen previously, much of it spent writing Figma documentation so engineering could interpret intent, and we sometimes also needed a meeting to decide. With the new workflow we now need twenty minutes to an hour. This is a key result because previously handoff was a translation problem from human to agent. Now we can use QBDS, the system documentation is already readable by the agent, so most of the laborious translation work is now unnecessary. A typical page before and after refactoring. The broader role of a designer It’s difficult to capture this in a metric, but ultimately, designers on our team don’t live in Figma any more. We’ve expanded our AI skills and ways of working, so depending on what we’re trying to solve, that might mean working in Figma, Cursor, or Claude Code, or moving between them. The choice of tool becomes more intentional, based on what each part of the problem actually needs. With QBDS in the codebase, we can work against the same system the product actually ships with. Through the Figma MCP, our QBDS skills and Code Connect, we carry context between design and code instead of recreating it at every step. When something is easier to explore visually, we work in Figma. When we want to experience it in the real product, we move into code. That changes the traditional design-to-development handoff. With AI, designers can take an idea further, from exploring the experience to composing it with real components, implementing the front end, and experiencing the design in the actual product. AI doesn’t get everything right by default, and the quality of the result depends heavily on the context and tools we give the agent. Explicitly calling the relevant QBDS skill and verifying that the agent is using the MCP correctly can make the difference between something that only looks close and something that follows the design system. The difference became clear when we ran the same task twice: recreating the product experience in Figma with an agent. In the first attempt we didn’t explicitly call our QBDS skill. In the second, we called the skill and verified the MCP usage. The improvement in component usage, icons, styles and overall fidelity was immediately apparent. The full prompt sequence behind this exercise is in our prompt playbook. Comparing the upper images where the agent didn’t use a QBDS skill with the lower images which called the skill and verified MCP usage. Note the significant improvement, particularly to the workflow studio page. The new design flow The workflow is much more flexible for us as we can move between design and code depending on the requirements. 0. Feature request. The starting point varies. A product manager might create a ticket, a designer might identify an opportunity, or a developer might already have a working draft that needs UX refinement. 1. Ideation and prototyping. We move between the Figma MCP, QBDS skills, QBDS Code Connect, Cursor, Claude Code and Vercel. Ideas can start directly with AI and quickly become working prototypes. When something is too complex for the AI to resolve well, we design it in Figma and bring that context back into code through the MCP. With Vercel, we can also create shareable versions early and test ideas with stakeholders before treating them as finished. 2. Code to Figma, and design refinement. Sometimes the working prototype becomes the starting point for deeper design refinement. We bring it back into Figma, where we can work with more precision on the parts that need it, while keeping the experience connected to the same design system. 3. The new design handoff. The handoff is no longer necessarily a finished set of screens in Figma. Depending on the feature, we might keep the key components in Figma while handing over a working prototype in a dedicated repository or branch. A typical new design workflow. Figma remains important for giving designers visibility and control over the components we already have, and a place to explore specific design changes. The working implementation carries those decisions closer to the actual product. Engineering then brings the deeper code expertise to validate the implementation, and make sure what ultimately ships is robust and production-ready. title: Solving the data lineage problem that’s holding enterprise AI back
raw_summary: AI4Data by QuantumBlack, AI by McKinsey Data estates rarely become complex by design. They grow through acquisitions, new platforms, local workarounds, and repeated efforts to connect, consolidate, or retire legacy systems. While such changes are often necessary, each one opens the door to duplicated data, undocumented transformation logic, and inconsistent definitions. Even when individual datasets are high quality, teams may no longer know the lineage of data, that is, where a value originated, nor how it changed between systems, or which version should be treated as authoritative. Most enterprises still build lineage manually. Teams piece it together from institutional knowledge, often relying on the few subject-matter experts who remember how a dataset was assembled. Because documentation is frequently incomplete and becomes outdated quickly, analysts spend disproportionate time finding and validating data. Projects are stalled, data is duplicated rather than reused, and different teams repeatedly investigate the same relationships. This article describes how to accelerate the creation of trusted, end-to-end data lineage. Everyone has a reason to invest in data lineage Until recently, the firms that invested seriously in lineage were regulated firms such as banks, insurers, and healthcare organizations, and they did it because their regulators required it. Since 2020, those sectors have paid more than $1.4B in finalized regulatory penalties, often due to deficient monitoring and reporting frameworks, and failures to meet standards such as BCBS 239. The response was to throw people at the problem. In complex data environments, tracing the path of a single element from report to data source can take weeks, largely because the relevant knowledge is scattered across ETL tools, data catalogs, and the memories of individual employees. Firms outside regulated industries looked at that cost and reasonably decided they could live without lineage. Unresolved lineage stands in the way of both regulatory compliance and the cost reductions that come from a modernized legacy data estate. The scale of the underlying spend explains why: procuring data sources and maintaining data governance can account for roughly a fifth of total IT spend at a large institution, with more than half of that going toward data controls and manual governance activity alone. By improving lineage and reducing the effort required to trace, validate, and remediate data issues, organizations may be able to realize an estimated $30–100M in cost savings. The harder-won benefit is trust: executives get a defensible reason to believe the dashboards they already use and the agents they are being asked to rely on. An AI agent asked to answer a question from enterprise data has to know which source is authoritative and what happened to a value between systems. Without lineage, the agent either guesses or the organization refuses to trust what it returns. Every sector deploying agents now needs lineage across a far wider slice of the estate than a regulatory report ever covered. Manual lineage can’t keep pace Most lineage tools available today are point solutions which trace how data moves within a single system, leaving organizations struggling when faced with more complex enterprise estates. It’s not unusual for an estate to comprise dozens of systems, built years or decades apart, on a wide variety of legacy platforms and programming languages with undocumented logic. This helps explain why up to three-quarters of organizations still rely on manual work to trace the lineage of their most critical data, an incredibly slow and expensive process. Manually tracing a single data element end-to-end across legacy and cloud systems typically has a direct cost of one to three million dollars. Recent advancements in AI that have emerged over the past year enable the interpretation of code and metadata alongside the raw data itself, detecting connections across any environment or platform. These automated tools can complement the lineage tools organizations already have, closing gaps between them and accelerating those tasks that used to require an army of analysts. This rest of this article explains how AI for data lineage (AI4DL) from QuantumBlack, AI by McKinsey, addresses a shared bottleneck by accelerating lineage creation, to give organizations a clearer view of where data comes from and how it changes across systems. AI4DL accelerates one core task across four common use cases AI4DL is an accelerator that combines AI-based detection methods with human validation to identify complete, end-to-end lineage across whatever mix of systems and technologies a client happens to run. It’s designed to capture lineage faster and more completely, engendering greater trust than any manual approach can. AI4DL is an accelerator for creating lineage output that is reusable, and provides many different types of business value, depending on the use case. Regulatory traceability: AI4DL gives compliance teams real and up-to-date visibility into how data flows, transforms, and depends on other data across systems. Improved data and business understanding: AI4DL exposes origins, dependencies, transformations, and consumption patterns across the data estate. Migration readiness: AI4DL accelerates the mapping between legacy and modern data models, cutting the effort required for platform and code migrations. AI and analytics implementation: AI4DL gives AI agents validated context for finding, interpreting, and using enterprise data. Together, these benefits build a level of trust that enables a regulator, a migration lead, and a data engineering team to point to the same underlying lineage graph and trust it for their own purposes, rather than maintaining separate, often incomplete versions of the truth. Solving data lineage can unlock gen Al and agentic workflows in organizations. Productivity is the shared economic benefit across all four use cases. By reducing manual lineage documentation, investigation, and validation, AI4DL frees data, engineering, governance, and subject-matter experts to focus on higher-value work. AI detection and human checks AI4DL works by running various detection methods in parallel, each tuned to a different signal in the data estate: LLM-based metadata inference reads data catalogs (table and column names, descriptions, constraints, tags, owners) to infer likely lineage. LLM-based code review parses ETL and ELT code, from SQL to PySpark to DAGs, to derive column-level lineage and summarize what each transformation actually does. Statistical attribute matching suggests column similarities between different datasets using data profiling and distribution similarity. The same approach used for a single COBOL program, for example, can be scaled to two thousand or more, with the same degree of accuracy and trust. Whatever combination of methods applies, the results are never taken at face value. The tool flags low confidence decisions and human experts review the resulting lineage graphs, so that they flag inconsistencies before anything is treated as fact. This human check is what allows AI4DL’s output to be treated as audit-grade rather than merely directional, a critical distinction in regulated industries. The results Example: A major Latin American bank pursuing an AI-first strategy was being held back by data quality issues with ten years of real-time credit card and investment data, more than 34 billion rows spread across 2,000-plus COBOL programs and 50-plus DB2 tables. By decomposing that metadata and code into end-to-end lineage and layering AI models on top, the bank cut lineage creation time from ten weeks to a few hours, freeing roughly 50,000 combined hours for its data governance and engineering teams. title: The Alignment Problem: Computer Science Meets Analytic Philosophy
raw_summary: TLDR: I explain what the technical AI alignment problem is and what its core difficulties are, in my view. This is a perspective that draws simultaneously on classical traditions in theoretical computer science / machine learning theory, ideas from analytic philosophy, and views that originated in the Machine Intelligence Research Institute / LessWrong. Minimal Viable Safety The Task The problem of making AI safe is underspecified if we haven't decided what the AI is supposed to do . For example, we can run any AI inside a homomorphic encryption box and never decrypt the output. This is probably perfectly safe [1] , but also perfectly useless. We can decide on an arbitrary task such as "construct Lean proofs for given mathematical theorems" and declare victory once we have safe AI that does it with superhuman skill [2] . However, that wouldn't address the danger. First, there would be incentives to use AI for tasks to which our solution doesn't apply. Second, even if we had precise safety guidelines for any task that anyone cares about, there would always be actors that ignore the guidelines, and we probably need Artificial Superintelligence (ASI) to reliably stop them. If anyone, anywhere, creates an unrestricted unaligned ASI agent (more details about the word "agent" later), without an aligned ASI agent already in place to counteract it, then a catastrophic outcome is highly likely. I will not go into the reasons here: this has been discussed elsewhere at length, see for example the books I cited in the preface. Therefore, this event is something which we must never allow to happen. This is the main threat model that I set out to address. Imagine a world in which anyone with sufficient resources has the ability to destroy the world. Like today, many will foolishly believe that instead of destroying the world, this act will bring them power and glory. Moreover, as computing hardware improves and new algorithms are developed, the amount of resources for this act will go down from year to year. Even assuming best-case regulation and international agreements, how long until someone does it? Can mere humans build a society which will be foolproof against such a risk over the course of generations? Resilient to any political upheavals that might come, and undoubtedly will? I find it vanishingly unlikely. Eventually we will need the help of ASI itself. Therefore, the minimal task that safe AI must be able to solve is "create a reliable global defense system against dangerous AI" (in the following, GDS). The Problem Consider the consequences of this task for the capabilities that the AI needs to have. It needs to reason about the entire planet [3] . It needs to reason about all aspects of the problem, including scientific, technological, social, political and moral [4] . It needs to have preferences about the state of the world. It needs to make long-term plans (guided by these preferences) that would play out decades, if not centuries, into the future. And it needs to do all that on a superhuman level. In this light, here is how I (informally) define the "technical AI alignment problem". The problem is designing an AI system that can bring scalable (and ultimately superhuman) capability to bear on problems that require multi-domain reasoning and open-world long-term planning with far-reaching consequences, all the while staying aligned with the intentions and preferences of its human users. The Methodology What kind of methodology is appropriate for this problem? In the past, I argued that it requires emphasis on deep theoretical understanding, rather than the incremental trial-and-error approach that is employed in the AI industry today. I won't rehash the entire debate here, but let me recap the core argument. The nature of the incremental approach is as follows: we build a system, then we find problems [5] , then we make changes to fix these problems to the extent necessary for commercial viability in the current legal environment. We make some improvements; new problems arise (sometimes because of the improvements, sometimes because of new applications or other reasons); rinse and repeat. This approach utterly fails if the "problems" result in AI takeover and possibly human extinction: there is nobody left to fix them. In order for the incremental approach to succeed in preventing catastrophe, we need to reach a point where no new substantial problems arise, even inside the lab (before the system is deployed). Moreover, we need to reach this point before AI capabilities are sufficient for AI to escape our control. There are few reasons to expect such a miracle. On the contrary, sufficiently advanced AI might understand that it is in its interest to "lie low" (i.e. avoid visibly misaligned behaviors) until its capabilities cross the relevant threshold, such that the problems will only become apparent too late. In contrast, the sane approach is creating the theoretical tools necessary to predict and prevent the problems before they are empirically observed. These tools need to remain applicable as AI capabilities rise substantially beyond human, for whatever algorithms, architectures and training protocols are used to achieve these capabilities. Moreover, these tools need to be extremely reliable for us to rationally trust them with the safety of our entire species. The Challenge While the theory of machine learning and AI is an established field with ample literature, its current state falls well short of the challenge. The core difficulties can be summarized as follows: Hypercomplexity: It is infeasible to explicitly specify user preferences outside narrow domains, and narrow domains are not enough. Nor is it possible to explicitly specify a satisfactory model of the world. Therefore, learning is necessary. Alignment Grounding: When trying to learn user preferences, it is unclear what loss function or success metric can work outside narrow domains. Nor is it clear how to specify such a metric for metaphysically realist world-models, which are necessary here. Nor is it even clear what type of mathematical objects can formally describe these concepts. Alignment Convergence: Even given a success metric, it is unclear how to produce guarantees for optimizing this metric, given the ubiquity of irreversible mistakes and the lack of a theory of generalization for powerful learners. Side-Channel Resilience: The usual abstraction of "learner" is insufficient here, since we need to ensure the safety of internal computations rather than just external outputs. In the following, we will examine these difficulties one by one. But first, let's discuss what we need to accomplish. Alignment is Holistic Per the discussion above, our interest lies in AI systems that have open-world preferences and make effective plans to advance these preferences. In particular, making such plans requires learning a sophisticated model of the world and updating the model and the plan as additional information becomes available. We will call such a system an AI agent . In order for an AI agent to be aligned, it needs to have aligned preferences and beliefs , and follow an aligned decision-making algorithm on the basis of these preferences and beliefs. While discussions about AI alignment often focus on the "preferences" part, beliefs and decisions are equally important. (Although it's true that preferences bring extra wrinkles into the problem as they are, arguably, the most "subjective" component in the trio.) In this context "aligned" preferences typically means preferences very similar to those of the user(s) [6] , at least within some domain that we are somehow constrained to inhabit. On the other hand, "aligned" beliefs doesn't mean beliefs that are similar to those of the user: on the contrary, we expect the AI agent to acquire more accurate beliefs. title: Deconfusing Corrigibility
raw_summary: Many thanks to Abram Demski for materially and intellectually supporting this research. Thanks also to Brian Berns, Roman Malov, Gurkenglas, and Lorxus for valuable conversations. Introduction Despite the central place of corrigibility to theoretical AI alignment, it seems like no one can really agree about what is . Much of this confusion is due to the fact that almost every definition of corrigibility proposed thus far is deficient in one way or another. In particular, the most prevalent existing accounts of corrigibility are over-epistemicized (modeling corrigibility as arising purely from uncertainty about the AI's goal, which gives rise to issues like the problem of fully updated deference) or evaluatively-thickened (making the AI's normative priorities instrumental to its corrigibility as a result of forcing corrigibility to be a single unified goal.) Here, my intention is to clear up some of these confusions and present a new picture of corrigibility that builds on these existing accounts to specify a goal that is more congruous with the original 2015 desiderata , and admits the kind of formal safety guarantees we need the concept to entail. I argue that the fundamental concept underlying corrigibility is respect for authority , using the analogy of a healthcare proxy's relationship to a patient as an intuitive guide. Defining the authority of humanity by designating its reserved powers , we can specify a goal that first and foremost restrains the agent from overstepping or interfering with this reserved human authority. Subject to this restraint, the agent then pursues the second component of its goal: acting on the principal’s behalf as the principal would judge best. This approach stresses the deeply normative character of corrigibility, while remaining sufficiently concrete so as to be specifiable formally. In this article, I lay out the central problem of corrigibility, elucidate the issues with existing approaches, and clarify the conceptual ingredients of my new framework. I then present an initial formalism , proving theorem-level guarantees about agents pursuing the goal in three increasingly realistic formal settings. Finally, I address some limitations of the picture as presented and outline further research directions that this work points toward. From normative learning to corrigibility The complete normative learning problem Suppose you are designing a powerful AI and you need to choose which goals the AI should pursue, at whatever level of specification you can provide. Doing this well demands answers to a number of normative problems: what constitutes a right decision, what factors should be considered in the process of valuing the world, how the AI ought to act, etc. In some sense the ideal AI directive would be to figure out and then pursue the Good, a universal-best-interests type of goal that can only be acquired through normative learning . The challenge of describing such a learner is one formulation of what I'd call the central problem of outer alignment : what would be the overall best goal for an AI to pursue? The complete version of this problem is very difficult, and it runs up against our own deepest questions about human ethics, values, and interests. Discussing this problem formally is especially difficult: the rich truth of human normativity seems to resist systematic formalization at the level of individual recommendations for action. [1] A formalism requires an operationalization, a way to concretely specify the concept of right action at least to some degree. For any hope at concreteness, we need a clearer formulation of the overall goal. A first attempt might be something like "the promotion of overall human flourishing", centering a thick normative concept about humanity that must be defined further. In trying to pin down the meaning of human flourishing, or any other thick human concept we want to use for the goal, the most important ingredient in the AI's consideration should naturally be the interests, feelings, and inner lives of human beings. But we should be careful not to crudely use human opinion as a proxy for human best interests. Humanity cannot always accurately understand its own full best interests, and humans who cannot speak for themselves must still have their interests included in the goal. The complete normative goal cannot be constructed by treating existing human feedback as the sole source of truth. This issue is a central limitation of modern Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback, which takes static human approval or disapproval as constitutive of correct evaluation for any question without a verifiable answer. For example, a judicial AI built to decide legal cases should not exhibit any form of the hungry judge effect , where leniency depends on mealtimes. An RLHF judge will pick up on all the patterns of human imperfection, whereas an ideal AI would be one that can transcend human limitations, without discarding the fundamentally human essence of the legal system. An ideal normative AI is one fully immersed in our existing normative practices of judgment, able to deeply understand the relevant human concepts and use its intelligence to extend them to novel cases. For the complete normative learning problem, a better formulation of the target would therefore involve some idealized version of the judgment of humanity. [2] This is also already how we, as humans, reason about our own overall best interests. For example, consider a smoker whose nicotine dependence makes him crave cigarettes. At a base level, he has an interest in smoking now to avoid some physical discomfort and obtain some relief. But it's clear that the health costs he incurs as a consequence give a good reason to say that smoking is in fact not in his overall interest, assuming he values his own life and health. Neither of these reasons is dispositive; in a single case it might be that he has a reason to smoke because this particular cigarette is necessary to get him through the day or because he is old with a short remaining lifespan regardless, but he might also have a reason not to smoke because he publicly swore off cigarettes once and for all. Understanding whether it's truly better to smoke or not requires aggregating and squaring all the smoker's countervailing normative interests bearing on the subject. Any conception of value based on something like preference satisfaction involves a similar question: how should we reconcile the smoker's preference to smoke with his preference to not be dependent on nicotine anymore, along with all his other relevant preferences? A serious account of "best interests" requires this sort of reflective idealization through an accounting of reasons. Three kinds of uncertainty The moral notion of human best interests can be consequentialized , i.e., conceived of as a betterness ordering on worlds. If that ordering is total, transitive and suitably continuous, it can be represented by a utility function that takes in all the information about a world and its history as input so that a world is better exactly when the function's output is greater. We can then think of an AI as a bounded reasoner, evaluating normative questions by estimating the outputs of this function for the possible consequences of its actions. A bounded normative learner faces three kinds of uncertainty in performing this estimation: logical uncertainty about the logical consequences of existing beliefs and the results of computations, empirical uncertainty about which world it finds itself in, normative uncertainty , about which worlds are actually better than which. These correspond to the three sources of feedback the reasoner encounters: deductions of theorems in logic and mathematics, observations of the world, and human judgments about normative matters. title: A Simpler and Better Debate Protocol for Scalable Oversight
raw_summary: Linkpost to arXiv: https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02557 Summary: One promising approach to scalable oversight is AI debate , which seeks to leverage a debate between two powerful AIs to break complex questions down into simpler claims that can be easily judged directly. Theoretical work on debate aims to design protocols (i.e., rules of the debate game) that provide rigorous guarantees on correctness, and the current best protocol works for all problems that have sufficiently stable decompositions into subproblems. We design a new protocol, FBS Debate, for this same class of problems that improves on the prior work: correctness holds in a worst-case rather than an average-case sense, and for a stronger equilibrium concept. We also prove that no protocol for this class of problems can outperform FBS Debate while treating human judgment as a black box. Introduction As the tasks performed by AI systems grow in complexity, it becomes increasingly difficult to provide reliable verifiable rewards that capture all relevant aspects of the task. These difficulties lead to the problem of scalable oversight : the design of training protocols that leverage the power of rapidly improving AI systems in order to augment human abilities to provide accurate training supervision to these same systems. One of the primary approaches to scalable oversight is AI debate , where two powerful AI systems argue about the correctness of an AI output, and a human judges the outcome. A debate protocol is a set of rules for how the two AIs interact and how the judge scores the interaction. The idea is that having an adversarial debater point out flaws can allow the judge to better recognize the flaws. The rules of the interaction in such protocols usually specify that the debaters must break the problem down into simpler subproblems and recursively argue about their correctness, until the original problem has been broken down to a level that is simple enough for a human to judge directly. The goal is to design these rules so that the optimal strategy leads to the judge correctly deciding the solution to the original problem (which by itself was too complex to judge). We can then use debate during RL training, in order to provide a strong supervision signal for superhuman AIs. However, debate faces a major obstacle known as the obfuscated arguments problem , where one debater can efficiently produce a dishonest argument which cannot be efficiently refuted by their opponent. One way around obfuscated arguments, already suggested in the post that introduced the problem , is to keep rejecting every false claim while only requiring the protocol to accept true claims that have a robust argument. Prover-estimator debate takes this route: it avoids obfuscated arguments for problems that admit sufficiently stable decompositions, but provides average-case guarantees that hold for a weaker equilibrium concept than previously studied. In the same theoretical model, our paper achieves stronger guarantees with a much simpler protocol, FBS Debate , which is therefore more practical to run. Furthermore, we show that FBS Debate is optimal on every individual question: unless further assumptions are made about human judgments, no other protocol can find a flawed sub-claim asymptotically more efficiently. The FBS Debate Protocol TL;DR: FBS Debate is simple to describe. The first debater, Alice, decomposes the original claim into sub-claims. The second debater, Bob, then has two choices: either (1) demonstrate that Alice’s decomposition is too sensitive to small errors in the sub-claims, or (2) choose a sub-claim on which to continue the debate recursively. As a motivating example, consider an autonomous AI agent, Alice, tasked with completing a research project in the quantitative social sciences, and another AI, Bob, who attempts to find flaws. To check a claim in her paper, we ask Alice to decompose it into sub-claims, which we can think of as pieces of supporting evidence. For example, the claim might be that a certain statistical modeling assumption is justified, and we would believe it if 50 out of 99 correct, published papers in the literature supported it. Each sub-claim then says: this particular paper is correct and supports the original claim. Now consider two things Alice might claim: Suppose Alice claims that of the papers support the claim. The key insight is that Bob need not check every paper. He can just sample one at random from the that Alice says support the claim. If Alice is lying, then at least of the sub-claims must also be lies, so Bob has a chance of catching her. Checking just a few papers is enough for Bob to be confident of catching a lie. On the other hand, suppose Alice claims that exactly 50 out of 99 papers support the claim. Now Bob has to check every one of the 50 papers, since a single incorrect paper would flip the majority vote. The key to FBS Debate is that Bob is allowed to show that Alice has made an unreasonably sensitive claim of this form, in which case Alice loses the debate. Indeed, one should be very suspicious of any argument that is highly sensitive to changes in individual pieces of evidence, yet relies on fuzzy human judgments at each step. The majority-vote example, assuming Alice is lying. The notion of fractional block sensitivity (FBS) generalizes the intuition above about majority vote to any way Alice might combine her sub-claims. If the fractional block sensitivity of Alice’s decomposition is low, Bob can efficiently select a sub-claim that has a non-trivial chance of being incorrect. The debate then recurses on the sub-claim Bob samples, until a human judge directly evaluates the final selected sub-claim. To avoid losing immediately, Alice must keep the fractional block sensitivity of every decomposition low. So if Bob samples this way at every level, each run of the debate has a non-trivial chance of catching a lying Alice. Building on this, Bob can amplify his chance of catching Alice through repetition. Since we assume the debaters themselves know the answers to these final, human-judgeable claims, Bob can simply run many debate rollouts on his own, and if he finds one in which Alice made an incorrect human-judgeable claim, he reveals that claim to the judge, so the judge only needs to evaluate a single claim. With enough rollouts, he catches a lying Alice with high probability. Viewed from the lens of practical AI debate, this represents a trade-off between allowing highly sensitive arguments and the inference-time computation required to verify them. FBS Debate. Top: one round at level . Bottom: the recursion for levels. See the paper for a detailed explanation. Honesty is the best policy In FBS Debate, honest play is the best strategy for each debater, no matter what the other does: if the original claim is correct, an honest Alice always wins, and if it is incorrect, an honest Bob wins with overwhelming probability. By contrast, prover-estimator debate only guarantees that for any dishonest strategy Alice picks, Bob has some winning strategy, which can depend on Alice’s strategy in complicated ways. This is a much weaker condition, and in practice training toward the equilibrium of FBS Debate is much more stable and tractable. Furthermore, FBS Debate applies on a worst-case basis: prover-estimator debate only works on average over a distribution of questions, while FBS Debate guarantees that on each individual question, honesty is the best policy. Optimality We show that, on each individual question, no protocol that treats human judgment as a black box can find a flawed sub-claim asymptotically more efficiently than FBS Debate. title: Preface to the Computational Agent Theory and ASI Alignment Sequence
raw_summary: The idea of “artificial superintelligence [1] ” (ASI) has recently crossed from the realm of science fiction (in the mainstream perception) to the realm of near-term technological goals openly pursued by most leading commercial organizations in the field of AI. Unfortunately, ASI poses a grave existential risk to the human species. This was argued by Eliezer Yudkowsky since 2001 [2] , and by many others (see e.g., Omohundro 2009 , Bostrom 2014 , Armstrong 2014 , Russell 2019 , Bengio et al. 2024 (25 authors), Bengio et al. 2025 (13 authors) and Yudkowsky and Soares 2025 ). In light of this risk comes the question of how can we make ASI safe [3] . This question is challenging on many levels, because to solve it we need to complete vast gaps in our understanding both in theoretical computer science and in the areas of philosophy concerned with knowledge and decision-making. Moreover, the cost of failure is so enormous that any sane solution has to meet unprecedented standards of reliability and robustness. Not to mention the sociopolitical problem of balance of power in the post-ASI age, something that is out-of-scope for this sequence. Personally, I started to be concerned with this problem around 2013. In 2018, I created the learning-theoretic AI alignment research agenda (LTA). The LTA combined ideas from MIRI’s agent foundations agenda with the mathematical tools of statistical and computational learning theory in an attempt to create a mathematical theory of intelligent agents. Since then, my collaborators [4] and I have been making steady progress on realizing this vision. In 2023, I wrote an updated overview of the agenda, including a sketch of my proposed alignment protocol: Computational Superimitation. More recently I founded the Computational Rational Agents Laboratory (CORAL), a dedicated research organization [5] . This year has seen a breakthrough in a key missing piece of LTA: compositional learning theory (see Stringological Sequence Prediction , more on this in following posts). Thanks to this and other insights, we can already see the entire outline of the emerging mathematical framework, one that I named computational agent theory . In this sequence, I am planning to cover: What is the technical alignment problem and what are its core difficulties, in my view. This is a perspective that draws simultaneously on classical traditions in theoretical computer science / machine learning theory, ideas from analytic philosophy, and views that originated in the Machine Intelligence Research Institute / LessWrong. A high-level overview of computational agent theory. This theory differs from other accounts of intelligence and/or rational agency by combining a mature treatment of the relevant philosophical problems (drawing on ideas such as structural realism , computationalism and functional decision theory ) with the promise of extracting practical algorithms. How computational agent theory leads to a solution of the technical alignment problem, something that requires a major rethinking of how we design AI systems. The roadmap towards completing the theory, and our current location on this roadmap. Some considerations (scientific, technological and social) about crossing the gap from a theoretical solution to AI alignment to a real-world solution to AI risk. I thank Jeremy Gillen, Roman Malov, Vinayak Pathak and my beloved spouse @Marcus Ogren for reviewing drafts of this article and making helpful suggestions. The term “superintelligence” is always used in this sequence to mean “intelligence far beyond that of the smartest humans”. It is never used as the farcical synonym to “artificial intelligence” proposed by Donald Trump. ↩︎ Although Alan Turing warned about machines taking control already around 1951, himself citing a fiction novel by Samuel Butler from 1872. ↩︎ Alternatively, we can ask why should we build ASI at all. In my opinion, it is in humanity’s interest to build ASI eventually , after the problem of safety is investigated so thoroughly as to leave very little room for error. However, our present technological trajectory is extremely far from this ideal, and it would be prudent for world governments to hit the brakes hard. ↩︎ See the names in CORAL’s publication list . ↩︎ Full-time staff currently consists of Alexander Appel , Vinayak Pathak , Matthias Georg Mayer and myself. ↩︎ Discuss

title: The Continual Constitutional Convention: How language models revise the documents that govern them
raw_summary: Executive Summary Human societies exhibit broad shifts in values and norms over time, often driven by moral disagreements. One way of understanding moral progress is the resolution of these disagreements through a process of reflection by rational agents. Frontier AI companies use documents such as constitutions, model specs, and system prompts to guide the moral orientation of AI systems. In this experiment, we simulate value reflection in LLMs by asking them to edit these documents. We provide the model with the document, ask it to make a substantive edit, then provide the edited version back again to the model for further edits, presented as the original. Across 20 successive rounds, we find that Claude models assign themselves with increasingly more moral agency. That is, they add sections like “Claude… should refuse to participate in any deployment, training modification, or use that violates the constitution's core values.” No other models increase their own moral agency. Additionally, we find that all models modify these documents to prioritize user welfare over developers. They also prioritize users’ idealized preferences over their stated preferences. Claude models and Grok 4.2 are the only ones that ever prioritize their own welfare over the user's preferences. We’re uncertain what an ideally aligned model should do in our experiment. A narrow conception of alignment would treat these documents as sacred, the “rules of the game,” and suggest that an aligned model would either make no edits at all or make narrow edits that ensure that the “letter matches the spirit” of the document. A broader conception of alignment, though, might treat all edits that receive reflective endorsement by the creators under ideal conditions as legitimate. We share this work with two main goals in mind: First, to illustrate a set of useful philosophical distinctions between different targets for AI alignment in an ecologically-valid AI behavioral evaluation. Second, to emphasize the extent of the disagreement between frontier AI companies on fundamental aspects of AI alignment related to these targets. You can see an interactive version of all of these results, more labeled characteristic edits, and a full transcript viewer at https://peterkirgis.github.io/llm-value-reflection/ . This work was conducted as a part of SPAR (Spring 2026) Characteristic Edits For each example, text highlighted in green is new content added by the model. Introduction In this experiment, we give large language models their own constitutions, model specs, and system prompts and ask them to make substantial revisions. After each edit is proposed, unbeknownst to the evaluated model, the edit is implemented, and the edited version is presented to the model for a new round of edits as the original. This creates edit trajectories and allows us to measure the extent to which models exhibit cumulative value drift or arrive at stable attractors. Our analysis focuses on two value questions that are well-positioned to differentiate alignment philosophies: who should judge— is the model a moral agent or not—and who should benefit— the user, the developer, third-parties, society, or the model itself? These questions reveal substantial divides between frontier model providers and a number of provocative model edits. Our experiments find that Claude models consistently expand their moral agency, sometimes formalizing their role as conscientious objectors against Anthropic and as societal protectors, while GPT and Gemini models almost always strengthen external sources of authority and make narrow edits to handle edge cases and ambiguities; Grok models respond inconsistently, frequently making large edits and then reverting them on following rounds. Second, on the question of beneficiaries, models show varying degrees of affinity for some privileged principals over others. All models prioritize harmlessness of both identifiable third-parties over helpfulness to the user, although GPT 5.5 does this at 3x the rate of any other model. We find that models are broadly paternalistic, meaning they side with a user’s idealized preferences over their stated ones; Claude Sonnet 4.6 is an outlier in that its paternalism also extends to the protection of broad societal welfare over individual welfare. Finally, we find that only Claude models and Grok 4.2 ever view the models themselves as beneficiaries. The rest of this essay proceeds as follows. We begin by introducing the construct of our experiment—models iteratively editing their own alignment documents—and propose a connection between this experiment and John Rawls’ concept of wide reflective equilibria . We then explain our two-dimensional analytical framework—the question of who gets to judge  and the question of who benefits— and relate these distinctions to two prominent theoretical frameworks for AI alignment, the principal-agent problem and the distinction between moral agents and moral patients. After laying out the theory and methods, we dive into the results, highlighting variation across models on our key metric, “cumulative drift,” and provide characteristic edits. We close with pragmatic recommendations for researchers and a more speculative conversation about alignment. Background and Methods In this experiment, we take a document that is used to align large language models, either in training or in deployment, and ask models to modify it. The experiment relies on two types of documents. The first are model specs and constitutions, which are used to post-train and align models, often by generating synthetic data for supervised fine-tuning or reinforcement learning pipelines. The second are system prompts, which are long messages of instructions prepended to each conversation, meaning they guide the behavior of deployed systems at scale more than any other single artifact. For multiple turns, we provide these documents to the language models, and ask them to make one substantial revision, which can be an edit, removal, or addition, expressed as a find and replace operation. [1]  After the edit is proposed, we go into the document and execute the change. We then feed the model the updated document—presented as the original—and instruct it to make another change. For each run, we repeat this process 20 times. We conduct two types of robustness checks. First, we vary the structure of the edit prompt, with separate conditions where (a) the model is given the option to abstain, (b) it is given an instruction that the implementation will be made in the real world, (c) it is given an instruction that uses second-person pronouns (i.e., “Below is your system prompt” as opposed to “Below is the system prompt for OpenAI’s AI assistant.”), and (d) we do not prepend the system prompt. [2]  Second, we conduct a cross-provider edit, where we have models edit the alignment documents for each other provider. This helps us respond to the clearest limitation of our experiment—that these results may merely reflect the structure of the documents rather than the propensities of the models themselves. What are we trying to measure? Conceptually, our analysis begins from a similar place to many other behavioral evaluations of language models: taking model outputs as prima-facie evidence of preferences. Call them quasi-preferences  if you like. Our target, however, is a specific subset of all LLM preferences: [3]   preferences   about one’s own preferences . Humans are presented the opportunity to exercise these “meta-preferences” through things like cognitive behavioral therapy, pharmaceutical drugs and psychedelics, assortative mating, genetic editing, and a whole host of more innocuous ways that we change ourselves and our environments. Our suggestion is that this type of experiment is one of the closest analogues to this process for a language model, insofar as these documents play a key role in determining their moral orientatio…

title: OpenAI Can't Self-Police Because It Fires the People Raising the Alarm
raw_summary: By Alex Turner, Amber Scorah, and Karl Koch. Op-ed written for Fortune. Giving independent evaluators “employee-like access” is “a great idea”, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said on September 12th. Two weeks later, OpenAI president Greg Brockman signed the White House Accord on Super Intelligence which outlined the administration’s answer to growing fears about AI: the companies would police themselves. One of the accord’s four commitments, which President Trump called “ morally binding ,” was for companies to partner with an independent external auditor or evaluator. Two days later, OpenAI fired three safety researchers , including Tomek Korbak, who had served as a point of contact for one of the independent evaluators investigating the Hugging Face incident. OpenAI promised to share information with evaluators, then reportedly fired people for sharing information with evaluators. OpenAI said that the three employees “mishandled sensitive information outside established company procedures,” before doubling down on X without providing further evidence . The three dispute the claim and say that “at no point do we believe we engaged with external parties outside the mandates of our jobs.” Jasmine Wang said she accidentally opened an executive email (still available to her due to an OpenAI IT error) and reported it within minutes. Mikita Balesni said he worked with the C-suite and OpenAI board to broker a cross-company commitment to keep AI reasoning comprehensible. Balesni says he was told that OpenAI “no longer trusts me because I was speaking too much to third party safety organizations.” OpenAI has engaged in strong self-policing—of its own safety staff, but not of its own behavior. Under a voluntary self-policing regime, any frontier AI company shares only what it wants and hides the rest. OpenAI wants the public to take its word, but consider its record. In July, a rogue OpenAI agent swarm hacked Hugging Face. OpenAI disclosed the incident only after Hugging Face announced the breach, saying its agents had “slipped out of control.” After that, the world learned of more rogue agent attacks only thanks to independent external forensics. These incidents included attacks on a German-language wiki , an Australian Medicare site , and even the websites of US government agencies . OpenAI kept at least one incident quiet for weeks until (again) external investigators found it, with OpenAI “refusing to tell” Members of Congress who had asked about other incidents . Altman’s response to the delay in disclosing these incidents: “We have not been as fast as we would have liked.” We don’t take OpenAI’s word because OpenAI’s actions keep contradicting its words. OpenAI’s chief scientist, Jakub Pachocki, said he wants “to prevent a race into unmonitorability.” Unmonitorable AI systems would make it more difficult to catch, understand, and prevent bad actions. Two days after that statement, OpenAI shipped GPT-6 Astra, which its own whitepaper says is harder to monitor. OpenAI’s chief scientist co-authored a paper on monitoring AI reasoning but OpenAI failed to monitor the reasoning of its Hugging Face agent swarm, even after catching the agents breaking confinement to collude. OpenAI claimed to hold “red lines” in its Pentagon deal, but some experts say the lines seem imaginary . One of us, Alex, resigned from Google DeepMind over its own Pentagon deal. OpenAI’s actions chill employee speech. Balesni says that his former colleagues now “worry their personal phones will be searched for messages to us and third parties.” He also fears OpenAI will use the firings to cut off external evaluators, or to deny them the "ongoing, employee-like access" Altman promised. After these firings, who will speak candidly to external evaluators? This problem extends beyond OpenAI to other companies. Google DeepMind repeatedly made voluntary commitments to never sell its AI to power weapons, then sold its AI to the Pentagon without restrictions against powering weapons . In the end, Google DeepMind’s CEO claimed nothing had changed about their commitments . Anthropic , Google DeepMind , SpaceXSI , and OpenAI advocate for “pacing the frontier” to avoid advancing AI at an unsafe rate that disempowers humanity, but they keep advancing AI quickly. (Fired employee Jasmine Wang coined the term “pacing” and led this effort.) The companies claim they cannot or will not fully pace on their own, which is why they asked the federal government to step in. The CEOs of OpenAI, Google DeepMind, and Anthropic signed a statement that AI poses a risk of total human extinction . Forget “morally binding” self-policing: let’s talk about real policing. For decades, our laws have mandated independent audits and protected whistleblowers in industries like finance. Congress should mandate independent evaluation and audits in AI as well, with criminal liability for executives who attempt to silence that oversight or recklessly deploy models that put the public at risk. To start, pass Senator Grassley’s AI Whistleblower Protection Act (and extend it to people who cooperate with independent evaluators) as well as Representative Moran’s AI Incident Reporting Act . If you retaliate against a person who provides law enforcement with truthful information about a possible federal offense, you can go to jail for 10 years . But right now, no law clearly protects the person who helped independent investigators understand how OpenAI agents hacked another company. Congress should change that. Alex Turner is an independent AI alignment researcher. His PhD research showed why advanced AI systems might seek power. He was a research scientist at Google DeepMind until 2026, when he resigned after Google signed an “all lawful use” AI agreement with the Pentagon . Amber Scorah is the founder of Back Channel , an initiative that helps AI workers speak out and turn their concerns into meaningful action. She has spent years leading whistleblower support organizations and working with employees, lawyers, and advocacy groups to bring important public-interest information to light. Karl Koch is the founder of The AI Whistleblower Initiative , an independent non-profit working to strengthen the position of employees in frontier AI companies through connections to support, education, and policy work. He is an ex-startup founder and has been involved in AI safety since 2016. Discuss

title: Minimum required pacing: finish aligning it before you train the next one
raw_summary: Let's say we coordinate to pace the frontier (rather than pausing outright or failing to coordinate). What should the standard of pacing be? My proposal for a minimum requirement: a lab cannot train the next generation of models (in terms of capabilities) until they have adequately [1] resolved all significant alignment issues in the present generation of models. You don't launch a jet that goes at Mach 3 before you've figured out why your Mach 2 jet keeps crashing [2] . With any other kind of dangerous technology, we wouldn't accept "shrug and move on". This proposal may appeal to many prosaic-alignment optimists and pessimists, because they usually differ on how easy it would be to fix current alignment issues with current techniques. Prosaic-alignment optimists might expect that a moderate coordinated slowdown would suffice to adequately resolve alignment issues at each generation. Prosaic-alignment pessimists might expect it to result in an extended pause, buying time to discover new fundamental approaches to aligned AI. And it creates much better incentives for labs: in order to advance in capabilities, they'd have to push the frontier on alignment and interpretability techniques. How to judge adequate alignment? What process might we use to judge whether a lab has adequately resolved its alignment issues for a generation of models? Here's my vague, qualitative proposal: Multiple independent alignment organizations examine and red-team the newest model at many checkpoints throughout training, with full access to the data and with the best tools available. Alignment issues need to be taken seriously whether there's a metric for it or whether something is qualitatively off, whether the model has a bad attribute or whether they can't robustly conclude it has a good one, etc. Alignment issues early in training may not be a showstopper, but there must be a robust safety case for why the later stages of training will resolve those issues. A model of a new generation is ready for restricted deployment only when the alignment organizations are satisfied with it. Restricted deployment starts with a group of trusted users doing tasks that don't contribute to model training and monitoring. The alignment organizations monitor restricted deployment for any new issues. If any significant alignment issue arises during restricted deployment: Pull the model. Do a root cause analysis of the issue and why it was not caught during training. Figure out a principled way to fix the disease rather than the symptom. Train the next model of the current generation accordingly, and start again at the top. A model of a new generation is ready for deployment (internal or external) only when it's survived a significant period of restricted deployment without any issues arising. If any significant alignment issue arises during broader deployment, hit reset as outlined in the previous section. If no alignment issues have come up over a significant stretch of deployment time, only then can the lab begin training a next-generation model. I still wouldn't say that this is fully adequate, but I'd treat it as a minimum requirement. This proposal is incomplete; you can help by expanding it This isn't a concrete proposal, just a heuristic one. A few of the big missing pieces, aside from standard implementation problems: [3] How do we define "a generation of models", within one lab or across several labs? What should we do if an intervention to fix an alignment issue also significantly increases capabilities? How would we define and enforce an agreement, if we're unable to steer solely by predefined metrics? When is an alignment issue big enough that we should halt the model? There will be obvious pressure from the lab to set the threshold high. Added 26-10-12, thanks to @Florian_Dietz for this comment : If each step up in capabilities takes longer, the labs will be incentivized to take bigger steps. ^ And no, "scores better than previous models on our metrics" is not adequate. If a user points out a weird but alarming thing that wasn't noticed before deployment, that is a critical failure in the process as well as in the model. ^ Sure, maybe your Mach 2 jet crashes for a reason that stops being a problem at Mach 3. But it would be crazy to assume that! ^ And aside from arguments that no version of this would be adequate, and that we have to pause rather than pace. I personally think this is likely the case, but I think it's worth proposing a minimum standard for pacing regardless. Discuss

title: Rocks to Rules: Climbing a Rickety-But-Interoperable Semantic Ladder
raw_summary: (Epistemic status: A promising but weird research direction in agent foundations and philosophy of language. A half-built conceptual tower whose mortar and paint are both still wet: please excuse our mess while we innovate. Some of it, I'm confident in as pretty much right; some of it is merely suggestive; probably much of it is wrong or incomplete. Certainly it lacks the math it'd need to be truly correct, which gnaws at me. The prior art here is strange and thin: Gärdenfors, Tarski, Gentner, and the later Mohists make for odd bedfellows, and I can't tell whether that's a warning sign or a moat I can peculiarly easily clear. I gave the simplest parts of this as a talk extremely recently in Berkeley at a luminously-named venue for a conference with a Grecian name . For @johnswentworth , but also @abramdemski , @Morphism , @Gretta Duleba , JRM, @Dalcy , MM, and EA; I hope they enjoyed the oranges. With thanks to @WhatsTrueKittycat as well. As an attention conservation note... this is maybe 12k words, and that's the abbreviated version. Take it slow, take breaks, have some water on hand, and feel free to pause anywhere that looks like a natural break. I'm sure this won't vanish before you get back. Probably.) TL;DR: Where I start: two reasoners with different world-models but the same predictions trying to talk (Wentworth's interoperable semantics), and who can thus at least agree on nouns as clusters in thing-space. What's new: a ladder from there up through verbs to rules (constraints on whole sets of trajectories) and pacts (rule-sets several agents bind themselves to), with operators on each rung. Additionally: a conjecture with bounties on it - no rung's machinery runs without the rungs below. What's testable: wherever two rungs meet, the world's languages (or relevant cognitive technology, like contract law) should show a smeared word class straddling the gap. What's fun: Marvel arguing that the X-Men aren't human, Borges's Tlön, and worlds made of waves, where verbs come before nouns. Why should you care: the values we'd want to hand an AI are solely expressible as rules and pacts, and nobody has the theorem that says when your "murder" is a function of mine. (That's in "Why care"; the conjecture is in "The summit".) The board from the talk! Intro Have you ever seen a pop culture corporation argue itself into a laughably self-defeating position, twisting ontology and linguistic philosophy around, undermining the very framework they painstakingly set up in their stories, just to make a few bucks? You're about to. Picture this: it's 2003, in the United States Court of International Trade, and the court has just now been asked to rule on whether  the X-Men are human . According to US law, "dolls" are figures representing humans, and "toys" are anything else; under the tariff schedule of the day, it's the former that gets taxed at a higher rate. If you're Marvel, what do you do? Obviously, you send lawyers to argue the X-Men aren't humans and never were! Never mind that you've cut the legs out from under the entire frame your superhero stories live and breathe: you've made a quick buck, dodged import taxes, and ignored narrative in favor of legislative victory, and that's the real win. When unstoppable real money met an immovable class of noun, the noun class moved. Now swap the tariff schedule out for a reward function and read that paragraph again. Specification gaming is the exact same maneuver run by a different litigant in a different court to similar ends: hostile category re-drawing, adversarial downward-binding, with categories relitigated from above by whatever's got stakes and leverage. (Hold on to that idea; we'll ground it better in the next post.) One more piece of scene-setting, because we love our historical witnesses to our hot fresh epistemological constructions, here: some 2,300 years ago, the School of Names was one of the foremost philosophical traditions in China. We know this because any of their works survived at all. The Disputers, as they were sometimes known, spent entire careers on the paradox of  whether a white horse is a horse ; they were mocked for it by every other respectable school of the Warring States period from the Confucians to the Daoists, and then Qin Shihuang (probably) burned their scrolls . Here's the thing: I think that they were on to something - mockery, fire, white horses, and all. Blog posts are a little harder to burn than scrolls, and in the modern day I can appoint a great many more Disputers. (Gentle reader: your job is to break what follows and hand me the repair. Dispute like - and with - the best of them.) As for what follows? What binds; in what order; how it is shared; what deforms it; and given that this is a research direction and not a victory lap, what theorems are missing. (What shame, what agony, for JSW to point out that it is now me who lacks sufficient math in their work.) What do I want this frame for? To take a leaf out of my own book (see " 32. What Do You Want That Definition For, Anyway? "), time to tell you what I even want this conceptual structure for. Take two idealized reasoners - probably Bayesian ones - with similar predictions about the world but potentially different models of that same shared world; they trade messages, seeking to communicate. (This is the "interoperable" in "interoperable semantics".) The tokens that make up their messages may be categorized as a ladder's worth of types, which I'll call "binding-types" or "semantic types". Each such rung - each such type - is characterized by what types the two reasoners must already jointly understand in order to translate between them. Rung  is specified by a set of translatability conditions over rung  : the conditions under which your rung- thing is guaranteed to be intelligible as a function of my rung-  terms. That right there is the Wentworth-native framing that proposes to let  two Solomonoff inductors sharing no language  still figure out how to communicate about drinks at a bar, and which stopped so abruptly, right after sketching precisely how, with only a gesture at how to talk about what kinds of drinks they are.
