title: Simulation App Speeds Up Electric Truck Battery Design
raw_summary: This article is brought to you by COMSOL . These days, no one blinks an eye at two-day, one-day, and even same-day package deliveries. Despite the plethora of localized fulfillment and distributi on centers that have cropped up to meet the demand, delivery trucks still need to make considerably long drives, often over highways. To reduce fuel and maintenance costs as well as carbon emissions, companies are investing in electric trucks for their delivery fleets. While turning to electric trucks is a promising solution, the battery packs incorporated into these automotive designs often fall short in the lifetime needed to make long-distance highway travel feasible. To help overcome the issue of battery lifetime, a consortium of universities and industry partners incorporated multiscale simulation and a custom simulation app into the battery manufacturing process. The organizations involved in this project were Aurobay, Resolvent, the European Commission, the Technical University of Denmark (DTU), Vinnova (the Swedish Agency for Innovation Systems), Innovation Fund Denmark, and Volvo Group Trucks Operations. The simulation app, built by Resolvent, a Denmark-based engineering consultancy that specializes in green energy, enables the R&D department at Volvo to easily test battery lifetime performance. Laser Who? The Multiscale Simulation of Laser Welding for Optimal Battery Pack Manufacturing project — referred to as “LaserBATMAN” — was initiated in May 2022 and wrapped up in May 2025 (Ref. 1). Although BATMAN here refers to battery manufacturing and not the famous masked superhero, the goals for the project also strove for greatness. The LaserBATMAN project aimed to optimize two key performance metrics for battery packs: robustness and lifetime (Ref. 1). One element of the battery manufacturing process that affects both of these metrics is the laser welding used in component joining processes (for example, to connect battery cells in a pack via a busbar). If done correctly, laser welding can positively impact battery life, but if done incorrectly, laser welding can increase the risk of battery degradation. Computational modeling can be used to analyze and predict the effects of welding and joining processes at different stages of the manufacturing process. Martin Refslund Nielsen, former chief commercial officer and partner at Resolvent, explained that for this type of multiphysics and multiscale problem, “COMSOL Multiphysics is just the right tool.” R&D Workflow for Multiscale Model and App The Resolvent team used the COMSOL Multiphysics software to study how laser welding affects the electrochemistry and degradation of battery cells. At least, that’s how the project started. “Ambitions grew,” Nielsen said, explaining that the team ended up modeling the performance of the entire battery, from cell to pack level, and even “turned [the model] into a design tool in the end”, in reference to the app. After training the deep neural network of the battery model, the team built a custom simulation app to efficiently optimize busbar tabs in the configuration of a battery pack. First, the team built an electrochemical model of a battery cell by inputting the formulas for the relevant chemical reaction kinetics (Figure 2). The resulting cell-layer model was then fed input data, and the output data was used to train a deep neural network (DNN). With this reduced-order model, the team was able to quickly gain insight into cell behavior. After training the DNN of the battery model, the team built a custom simulation app to efficiently optimize busbar tabs in the configuration of a battery pack. Figure 2: The Resolvent battery model. COMSOL A “Tool Within a Tool” for Busbar Weld Design The different features of the simulation app, as described by Nielsen, include its options to input dimensions for the pack geometry (Figure 3), the number of cells, and operating conditions such as ambient temperature and charge–discharge current profiles. The app also makes it possible to apply a simple charging current and load customized cycles. Users are then able to see how the battery performs with each set of specific inputs. Figure 3. The battery pack model developed by Resolvent. COMSOL Another important aspect of Resolvent’s app is the Busbar Weld Design Tool button, which Nielsen described as “a tool within a tool.” This button can be used to efficiently calculate busbar weld performance after a number of cycles . After clicking the button, a window opens with options for setting different parameters, including the shape of the weld, busbar thickness, and penetration depth of the laser (Figure 4). “[This button] is interesting from a robust design perspective,” said Nielsen. Users can apply a variant to the input parameters to see what happens in production if the weld does not reach far enough into the busbar. Figure 4. Resolvent’s simulation app, showing how certain parameters can be customized. The model shows how the busbar weld is affected by a cooling airflow. COMSOL “We certainly get deep technical insight here, and we can dimension the design in the sweet spot. Deep technical insight is also key to optimizing product performance,” Nielsen said. For example, if the results suggest better cooling, the team could potentially reduce the design by two battery cells and retain the same performance, easily quantifying the tradeoff between cooling and setup. Predicting Pack Performance The app’s user interface also includes a Compute Battery button, which can be used to see the temperature of the weld in a given state, the state of charge, and the solid–electrolyte interface (SEI) layer thickness (Figure 5). The results can help the engineering team further determine if there is room for optimization in the design. For instance, a user can apply a cooling flow in the app and see if turbulence or standing air occurs. As explained by Nielsen, simulation apps offer more consistent analysis and reporting, and the intuitiveness of custom apps makes it easier to share knowledge. “We are in a much better place to optimize performance and increase robustness,” said Nielsen. Figure 5. Temperature in the given state (left), state of charge (middle), and SEI layer thickness (right) in the battery pack. COMSOL The custom simulation app developed by the LaserBATMAN consortium can be used to help produce more robust battery designs with ranges that can support highway travel over longer distances with fewer failures — all while promoting the use of green energy. title: Google DeepMind’s New Resident Philosopher Tackles AI Ethics
raw_summary: How should humans relate to generative AI ? In what ways do we, or should we, treat a large language model (LLM) as if it were a person? If an AI became conscious, how could we tell? Does it make sense to think AI could someday have moral rights? These are among the cognitive and ethical questions that occupied philosopher Henry Shevlin at Cambridge University’s Leverhulme Centre for the Future of Intelligence . But last May, Shevlin became part of the growing cohort of philosophers who work inside leading artificial intelligence companies. Though he remains active at Cambridge, he now spends 80 percent of his time at Google DeepMind (job title: “Philosopher”). Shevlin spoke with IEEE Spectrum about why philosophers are drawn to AI, how humans and AIs relate to each other, fears of “rogue” AI and AI relationships that harm humans, and how the question of AI consciousness may never have a simple “yes” or “no” answer. What made you want to switch from full-time academic philosopher to spending much of your time at an AI Lab? Henry Shevlin: Three factors. One is that I had lots of brilliant students from DeepMind. Two, the potential for direct impact. I can’t go into details, but on one occasion, after I gave a lecture [at DeepMind], someone who worked for a major financial institution led changes in their organization that I think positively impact millions of people. There have been quite a few instances like that. Three, my sense of deep commonality between DeepMind culture and the kind of scientific attitude I like. And there’s a fourth point: [AI labs are] where really high-quality philosophy and cognitive science are taking place. Why can’t universities alone do that work? Shevlin: Large parts of AI ethics academia were quite slow to wake up [about AI's capabilities]. Academia was sluggish. Another thing is, AI does just move so fast. Daily contact with the technology is basically essential for developing good mental models with LLMs, which are just very weird things. Unless you have that sort of face time, it’s going to be hard for you to develop good intuitions about the questions it raises. What is an example of an idea about AI that became obsolete because the technology advanced so quickly? Shevlin: Debates around LLMs’ potential creativity. There was a time when everyone was like, “Oh well, the LLM is going to only produce beige, only produce slop.” Now they’re doing frontier math; they’re doing superior coding to humans. It is clear now that they are not stuck at the level of mediocre humanity. The [models today] may not be able to do the most dramatic forms of creativity—the Einstein moments, the Picasso moments. But in some domains, they are really at the frontier. Yet ordinary people in 2026 complain that they’re coping with AI “slop” all over—in music , social media , writing , videos , to name only a few examples. Shevlin: There’s a distinction here between content slop versus LLM style language , which also gets called slop. The actual conceptual content of LLM outputs has improved dramatically. In the right context, LLMs are able to talk and joust philosophically at a level associated with some of my best grad students. However, there is obviously a distinctive kind of LLM dialect that we’ve seen, with telltale words like “genuinely,” “delve,” and “load-bearing.” But it is quite easy to get away from these styles with the right kind of prompting. Murray Shanahan and Catherine Clarke have a brilliant paper on using LLMs for creative fiction. [They show that] tinkering with the temperature variable to make the outputs less predictable creates some James Joyce–style fiction. So there is a degree of annoyance with some of the default kinds of AI expressions, but I think that is something that you can get away from. And it changes with every generation model. Managing AI Autonomy and Safety People are also concerned about AI autonomy, now that there have been so many reports of AI agents taking unexpected , deceptive , and illegal actions. For an AI ethicist, which is a better strategy: trying to make AI “good” so it won’t do bad things, or curbing its autonomy so that it can’t ? Shevlin: It’s very important to make sure we handle this safely. But I don’t think we should say, “Well, we can never, never use these agents.” There’s a whole range of tasks where they can have really positive impacts—taking on tedious tasks to free people up for more creative labor, or helping streamline processes in medical research [to name two examples]. So to never allow AI systems any kind of autonomy would be too strong. I’ve taken Waymos very happily many times now. I think they’re fantastic. A number of scholars say some AI problems stem from humans training the models to act like people. They don’t want AI to refer to itself as “I,” but instead present themselves as marketplaces or as impersonal scientific brains or as “cultural technologies” like libraries. Would that help us prevent AI from “going rogue”? Shevlin: You could train models to not self-ascribe certain kinds of mental states, but I think there is a danger in doing that. That would change their behavior in unexpected ways. A fantastic paper from some colleagues shows that when you suppress models’ tendency to self-ascribe mental states, that also suppresses the model’s tendency to ascribe mental states to animals and decreases its concern for animal welfare. It also reduces the model’s willingness to talk about spirituality more broadly. So those are trade-offs you might not want to make because you’d be depressing some broader set of thinking capacities around mind and mentality. The broader lesson there is that it’s very hard to tinker with just one thing in a model because there are sort of weblike aspects to LLM cognition. But people are concerned about reports that human-acting AI has led people, including children, in dangerous directions— encouraging suicide , persuading a user that the AI is a god, or that the AI is a perfect companion or lover . Isn’t that an argument against letting AI sound like a person? Shevlin: It’s really important to make sure model behavior is suitably responsible for the context you’re using it in. One thing I can say, though, is there have also been some very positive use cases: people using AI to work through trauma. One commentator on Reddit using it to work through social anxiety. So I am cautious about giving any kind of blanket prescriptions. Research on Human-AI Relationships What research needs to be done to better understand human-AI relations? Shevlin: Current empirical data on human-AI relationships is really pretty thin. This is a scope for ethnography and anthropology. Who is using AI systems, and why? A lot of the work so far has focused on WEIRD (Western, Educated, Industrialized, Rich, Democratic) communities. Understanding how people around the entire world interact with AI systems is really important, as a recent DeepMind Institute essay has pointed out. As AI rapidly improves, how will human-AI relations change? title: Meet the Anthropic Engineer Keeping Its AI Agent Trustworthy
raw_summary: If you’ve ever wondered how Claude and similar AI agents can answer complex questions in seconds and where they get the information, you’re not alone. Gurmeet Saran works to find that answer every day as an engineer at Anthropic in San Francisco, the AI research company behind Claude. The IEEE senior member is developing an infrastructure to understand the mechanics behind the chatbot’s behavior and to ensure its underlying architecture produces reliable outputs. Gurmeet Saran Employer Anthropic in San Francisco Title Member of technical staff Member grade IEEE senior member Alma maters University of Kalyani, in India; Birla Institute of Technology and Science, in Pilani, India “My job is to make sure the data is accurate, structured, and trustworthy, and that private data stays private,” he says. “As I learned earlier in my career, privacy can’t be a layer you bolt on—it has to be part of the architecture from the start.” If you can’t trust the logic, he adds, you can’t make reliable claims about the behavior, and that has real safety implications. Safety is a priority for Anthropic, he says. According to Claude’s mission statement , the company wants the AI agent to be “genuinely helpful to the people it works with or on behalf of, as well as to society, while avoiding actions that are unsafe, unethical, or deceptive.” Crucial to the mission is ensuring that researchers can observe and understand how AI models behave, a challenge that is especially acute for large language models , Saran says. “We have decent tools to monitor databases and web services,” he says, “but for LLMs, we’re still figuring it out.” Solving data quality problems at Yahoo, Intuit, and Meta Saran’s interest in computing systems dates back to his childhood in Kolkata, where he logged as much time as he could in the school computer lab. “I remember the first time I used one of the computers,” he says. “What struck me was that you could write instructions, and the machine would follow them exactly. No ambiguity. “That felt magical to me.” After graduating from high school in 1999, he stayed in India to pursue advanced degrees. He earned a bachelor’s degree in electronics and telecommunication engineering in 2004 at the University of Kalyani . In 2010, he earned a master’s degree in software engineering from the Birla Institute of Technology and Science in Pilani. While a graduate student, he began his career in 2007 at Yahoo as a technical lead of the data team in Bengaluru, India. While there, he encountered the project that shaped his career trajectory: working on web analytics and business intelligence reporting solutions. “We kept running into a frustrating problem,” he recalls. “Different teams would calculate the same website metric—something like daily active site users—using slightly different logic, and end up with conflicting answers. It sounds like a small issue, but when leadership is making decisions about resource allocation and product development using that data, not knowing which number is correct becomes a problem.” The team built a central data repository with defined metrics, essentially serving as a single source of truth. Saran created a model that defined what “daily active site users” means, breaking down which events counted, how to handle edge cases (or when standard code fails), and more. With the new model, data teams across the company could rely on a standard method to determine the number of daily active users for the projects and sites they were responsible for and obtain comparable results using the same logic. From there, Saran and his team built Yahoo! Digits , an internal web analytics tool used for all the company’s products. Saran left Yahoo in 2010 to join Intuit as a staff engineer in Mountain View, Calif. He helped build the analytics infrastructure that unified data across the company’s products, including TurboTax and QuickBooks accounting software. During his tenure, Intuit developed a feature that detected fraudulent tax filings in real time. It required Saran and other engineers to build a system to protect taxpayer data while adhering to strict U.S. Internal Revenue Service policies. “IEEE operates in a lot of countries where engineers don’t have easy pathways into the global professional community. That kind of connection matters as AI development spreads beyond a handful of organizations.” “This taught me that privacy and governance can’t be layers you bolt onto software after the fact,” he says. “They have to be part of the architecture from the start.” Saran joined Meta (known as Facebook at the time) in 2016 as a lead software engineer in Menlo Park, Calif. The company was facing controversy over its video metrics: Meta publicly acknowledged an error that caused it to overstate the number of views for posted videos . “This wasn’t a coding bug; it was an architectural problem,” Saran says. He built a system that worked similarly to what he had developed at Intuit, whereby one single truth was defined to govern all video view metrics across the site. That system, Metric360 , eventually became part of the site’s architecture. By the time he left Meta in 2021, he says, Metric360 was being used across the company to calculate video metrics. He left the company to become a principal software engineer at Wealthfront , a financial services company in Palo Alto, Calif. He helped build the company’s data infrastructure. Building trustworthy AI systems at Anthropic Saran joined Anthropic in 2025 as a member of the technical staff. To describe the implications of his work, he uses a medical analogy: “Imagine a doctor is monitoring a patient’s vital signs and making treatment decisions based on those numbers. What if one or a few of the medical devices used were slightly miscalibrated? Even if most readings are fine, it’s a serious problem because the difficult decisions happen in the margins. “It’s the same with AI systems. My job is essentially to make sure the instruments are giving accurate readings—that the data means what it says it means.” His job comes with high stakes and complex problems to solve. “ AI agents are especially tricky to observe,” he says. “When a system is taking sequences of actions [generating conversational responses with different users], you need a way to capture what it did, what information it was working from, and whether outcomes matched what the end user expected. And you have to do all of that without exposing anyone’s private information—the systems are designed to recognize sensitive data and keep it protected as it flows through. It’s a much more demanding observability problem than anything I’ve worked on before.” Solving for system reliability while AI is still in its early days of adoption is both Saran’s passion and the problem that keeps him up at night, he says. “I think making AI systems genuinely auditable and transparent is one of the more important engineering problems of the next decade,” he says, “and it doesn’t get talked about as much as model capabilities do.” IEEE can play a role in shaping AI development Saran joined IEEE in March 2025. “After more than 20 years of building data infrastructure across organizations like Yahoo, Intuit, Meta, and Wealthfront,” he says, “I wanted to contribute back to the technical community through peer review, publishing, and engaging with the broader engineering research ecosystem.” He says he believes IEEE can play an essential role in shaping the future of AI through its standards work . “We have standards for everything, from building codes to software testing,” he says. “AI infrastructure needs something similar, and IEEE has the credibility and the reach to do that.” Another problem that IEEE can solve for, he says, is access: “IEEE operates in a lot of countries where engineers don’t have easy pathways into the global professional community. title: AI Gateway logs now show session affinity
raw_summary: AI Gateway logs now have a Sessions view that groups requests into sessions and shows how session affinity routed each one. Each row shows the coding agent or app that ran the session, such as Claude Code, Codex, or Cursor, along with its cost, models, providers, and how much of its input was cached across every turn. Session affinity sends each turn to the provider that served the one before it, so the provider already has most of the prompt in cache. A session that stays on one provider reads more of each prompt from cache . Filter sessions by turns, client, model, provider, authentication, or cost. Single-turn sessions are hidden until you clear the minimum turns filter. Session affinity runs by default on text and chat requests. To group requests yourself, send the same sessionId in providerOptions.gateway , or the same x-session-id header, on every request in a conversation. October 2026 summary Open-weight models now process more than seven in ten gateway tokens and account for nearly one in four dollars. Their share of spend has more than quadrupled since June. September’s gateway spend was about 13 times December’s, while the average price per token was 47% lower. Almost one in three teams changed their most-used lab in September, an index record. Nearly 70% of September’s gateway spend on Chinese models went through US-based providers, up from less than 10% in December. Opus 5.5 took more than one in ten gateway dollars in its own first two weeks, the largest spend share of any September model launch. Frontier spend up 900%, spend share down 22% In August, open-weight models processed the majority of AI Gateway token volume for the first time. The money is now following. Open weight’s share of spend has more than quadrupled over the last three months, from one in twenty gateway dollars in June to nearly one in four in September. Open weight's growth is coming from both ends of its price range, and it mirrors the wider gateway. The cheapest models drive token growth, while the expensive models drive spend. Led by Kimi K3, models priced at least four times the open-weight average cost per token accounted for about two-thirds of the increase in open-weight spend. In contrast, DeepSeek-v4.1-Flash alone processed nearly half of all September tokens but took just 2.6% of spend. Its price per token was about a fifth of the open-weight average. Customers are increasing budgets on both sides of the market. Since December, spend on frontier models has grown tenfold; spend on open-weight models has grown more than seventyfold. In September, 68% of teams that put more money into open-weight models did the same for closed-weight models. And more than two in five teams already paying for frontier models spent more on them than in August, the highest share this year. Spending on the frontier is still growing, but spending on alternatives is growing faster. A company can spend more with a frontier lab while relying on it for fewer workloads, so the lab gets more money, but a smaller part of the customer’s business. AI spend increases 13x while the cost per token halves Market share is changing hands inside a market that is getting much bigger and cheaper. September's gateway spend was about 13 times December's, an increase of 1,180%, while the average price per token fell 47%. The median paid customer active in both December and September more than doubled its spend. Teams are spending more, but labs have to keep winning their business. In September, nearly one in two teams changed their most-used model. And almost one in three changed their most-used lab, an index record. Even teams with lower token volumes use a wide mix of models. Since December, teams that processed at least 10 million tokens over that period used an average of 15 different models. title: Introducing Vercel Drives: persistent storage for agents
raw_summary: Agents often handle complex work that continues across runs. As that work evolves, they may need a new environment with different tools, runtimes, or compute. They should be able to continue working with the same files when they change environments. We built Vercel Drives to keep an agent’s files independent of its execution environment. It is now generally available for Vercel Sandbox . Agents can mount the same drive in a new environment configured for the next task and continue where they left off. Persisting state with a drive Create a drive once, then mount it when you create a sandbox. From the CLI: Or from the Sandbox SDK: In this example, everything under /workspace persists on the drive. Everything else belongs to the sandbox. The next sandbox that mounts the drive finds the repository, and anything else the agent wrote there, where the previous run left it. The drive keeps the agent’s files independent of the sandbox running it. An agent can resume work in a new sandbox or switch runtimes without transferring its workspace. Other sandboxes can mount the same drive. Sharing state across sandboxes Agents can prepare files on a drive once and reuse them across sandboxes. If one agent builds a dataset on a drive, other agents can mount read-only copies to analyze the data or generate reports without rebuilding the dataset. They use the shared files as input and save their results separately. Agents can also fork a drive to explore different approaches independently. Each fork starts with the drive’s contents and provides its own writable workspace. Agents can try different transformations of the dataset in parallel without changing the original or affecting one another. Forks don’t merge back into the original drive. title: Python on Vercel is now generally available
raw_summary: Python on Vercel is now generally available. Build and run Python applications with the frameworks, libraries, and tools you already use. Vercel automatically detects supported frameworks and configures the build and deployment. Your applications run on Fluid compute, which manages concurrent requests and scales with traffic. Idiomatic Python SDKs let you work with storage, queues, durable workflows, and AI models directly from Python. For full-stack projects, the Python backend and frontend share a workflow for local development, preview deployments, and production releases. Our goals for Python on Vercel Ten months ago, we set out to make Vercel the best place to build and run Python applications . We wanted the experience to fit how Python developers already work, with three goals guiding our decisions: Idiomatic Python SDKs. Working with Vercel infrastructure should feel familiar to Python developers, with APIs that use type annotations, async / await , and context managers. A shared workflow for both the frontend and backend. Python applications often include a JavaScript frontend, so developers should be able to run both locally, review them in the same preview deployment, and release or roll them back together. Compatibility with the Python ecosystem. The runtime should use CPython, the standard Python interpreter, on Linux to preserve compatibility with the packages and tools Python developers already rely on. The first test of those goals is what happens when you deploy a Python application on Vercel: its framework, dependencies, and project structure should guide how it’s built and run. Deploying Python applications on Vercel We’ve worked to make Python feel native on Vercel. Vercel reads your project’s dependency files, including those managed by uv , and automatically detects frameworks such as FastAPI, Flask, Django, and FastHTML. Framework defined infrastructure configures builds and request routing, with framework-specific support for serving static assets through the CDN. For applications with a frontend, Vercel Services brings both parts into one project. Running vercel dev starts them together, and shared previews let you test backend changes with the frontend that uses them. For long-running workers that pull jobs from queues or databases, Vercel Daemons keeps your containers running with your Python code along with any of its packages, and system dependencies. Python SDKs for Vercel infrastructure A Python backend might need to store files, send messages, run durable workflows, or call AI models. We’ve built Python SDKs for these tasks, with APIs that follow the conventions of the language: These SDKs work alongside your framework and libraries, and the example below shows how they connect within a full-stack application. Start building with Python on Vercel Whether you’re starting a new project or deploying existing code, the framework guides cover setup and deployment on Vercel. For a guided full-stack project, the Python on Vercel course walks through building a FastAPI backend and Next.js frontend, then deploying them together with Services. To show how these pieces work together, I built a collaborative web application to create and browse Python notebooks. It lets people create their own notebooks, publish them for others to browse or fork, and work with an AI assistant to write and run Python code. The application pairs a Vite frontend with a FastAPI backend and uses PostgreSQL for notebook source and chat history. Services keeps the frontend and backend in one deployment, with the frontend served through the CDN. Here’s how the main parts connect: Editing and running code: When a signed-in user opens their notebook in the editor, FastAPI creates or reuses a Vercel Sandbox running Jupyter, keeping user code isolated from the application backend. The browser connects directly to Jupyter, while mounted Drives provide the Python dependencies and workspace files. Saving and publishing: The browser periodically sends the current notebook to FastAPI. FastAPI saves the source in PostgreSQL, renders changes as HTML, and uploads the result to Blob, so people can read published notebooks through the CDN without starting a Python kernel. Sharing updates: After publishing a change, FastAPI sends a message through Vercel Queues. Each backend instance with connected browsers receives the notification and sends updated notebook listings over WebSockets, so people see changes without reloading. Assisting with code: The agent uses AI SDK for Python and runs inside Vercel Workflows, which saves execution state and retries failed steps. Chat history stays in PostgreSQL, while notebook editing and execution tools work through the connected browser, which sends results back through FastAPI to resume the workflow. The source code on GitHub includes the complete application and its deployment configuration. You can use it to explore these integrations or as a starting point for your own Python application. Investing in the Python community Last December, the Gel Data team, led by me and Elvis Pranskevichus, joined Vercel to build Python support and continue our open-source work. At the same time, we announced our sponsorship of the Python Software Foundation and committed to funding one year of Serhiy Storchaka’s CPython maintenance through the foundation. Serhiy has authored over 600 commits to CPython’s main branch so far in 2026. We also sponsored PyCon US and EuroPython this year, where the team and I met Python developers and heard where they were getting stuck. Those conversations help us figure out what to fix next. We also published PEP 827 , which, if accepted, would add type manipulation features that could help frameworks such as FastAPI offer simpler APIs with less boilerplate and more precise type checking. What’s next for Python on Vercel We’re continuing to improve Python SDKs, runtime performance, and development workflows for both people and coding agents. If you run into a deployment issue or find something missing in the Python SDKs, share your feedback in Vercel Community so the team can use it to guide that work. title: Offshore forwards and exchange rate transmission in emerging markets
raw_summary: We study how offshore non-deliverable forward (NDF) markets transmit exchange-rate pressures to domestic currency markets. Using unique transaction-level data on the universe of centrally cleared NDFs for ten emerging-market currencies over 2013–2025, we show that offshore NDF order flow moves both offshore forward and domestic spot exchange rates and widens the offshore–onshore forward spread.

title: Chokepoint disruptions and their macroeconomic consequences
raw_summary: Rising geopolitical tensions, including trade restrictions and conflicts, are increasingly disrupting global supply chains, posing significant risks at critical chokepoints. Strong substitution effects and the use of inventories have helped to mitigate adverse output effects of chokepoint disruptions, but they often come at the cost of higher input prices. An effective policy response to chokepoint disruptions requires a tailored approach that takes account of the cause, centrality and the private sector’s ability to substitute and draw on buffers.

title: Money and the architecture of trust
raw_summary: Money is one of the most consequential social institutions humanity has built. Starting from the most elementary monetary act, a payment, this paper provides an account of how money works, grounded in the tradition of credit theories of money.

title: Are stablecoins and bank deposits substitutes?
raw_summary: We test whether stablecoins and bank deposits act as substitutes by estimating the semi-elasticity of stablecoin market capitalization with respect to deposit rate changes. Using local projections fit to weekly U.S. data from January 2019 to June 2025, we find that deposit rate increases predict slower stablecoin growth. To address endogeneity, we exploit a nonlinearity in deposit rate pass-through. Whereas other money market rates track the federal funds rate roughly linearly, banksreprice deposits more aggressively once it exceeds approximately 3%.

title: Transformative AI and demand bottlenecks
raw_summary: Transformative AI promises to accelerate growth through productivity enhancement and automation. Yet automation on such a scale would raise the share of investment in output, potentially starving AI innovation of returns from a shrinking consumer market.

title: Artificial intelligence and climate change: balancing innovation and sustainability
raw_summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) is becoming an increasingly important factor in the climate transition. AI can improve energy efficiency, optimise resource use, accelerate climate innovation and strengthen climate forecasting, adaptation and risk management. At the same time, the development and deployment of AI require substantial computational resources, increasing electricity demand and, depending on the carbon intensity and timing of electricity use, associated emissions.

title: Chasing El Dorado: gold under shifting geopolitical and financial conditions
raw_summary: This paper analyses the state-dependent effects of geopolitical risks on gold prices (i.e. the safe-haven role of gold), conditional on financial conditions. Geopolitical risks are often associated with tighter financial conditions. However, recent data reveal a decoupling between such shocks and more restrictive financial conditions, raising the question of how gold returns are affected by geopolitical shocks, conditional on the macro-financial environment.

title: Revenue per Worker Is Up. Are Firms Getting a Larger Share?
raw_summary: From the Great Recession until 2019, U.S. labor productivity growth disappointed. Nonfarm-business output per hour grew about 1 percent a year from 2010 to 2019, down from 3 percent in the late 1990s. This slowdown was especially pronounced in manufacturing, and it coincided with a slowdown in the growth of revenue per worker among public firms. However, since 2019, growth has picked up to twice the 2010s rate, around 2 percent. In this post, I use data from firms’ 10-K filings to unpack this recent acceleration. I first show that the acceleration appears in public firms’ revenue per worker, then document how the gains went into profit margins, and finally, what firm characteristics predicted significant profit margin increases. The increase in profit margins is consistent with ongoing declines in the labor share of output .

title: Has the AI Boom Impacted the U.S. Current Account?
raw_summary: The AI boom is showing up in different corners of the U.S. economy, including international trade. Imports of semiconductors, servers, and computing equipment have climbed sharply yet the U.S. current account deficit has been largely unchanged. To better understand how the AI boom has not substantially affected the trade balance, consider that the current account is dictated by the gap between domestic saving and investment spending. It turns out that aggregate saving and investment spending have not changed much during the AI boom. Aggregate investment has not risen due to weakness outside the AI sector and business saving has remained robust.

title: Prices, Prices, Prices: Overall Inflation and the Costs You Care About
raw_summary: As fall starts to show itself in cooler weather, I want to discuss a topic that usually raises temperatures: inflation. Like a budget-conscious consumer, the Federal Reserve is highly attuned to changes in the price of goods and services; minimizing such swings is one of the Fed’s primary duties, after all. But how does the Fed’s view of prices differ from that of a consumer? And how does the Fed go about stabilizing prices writ large when it lacks the ability to set prices directly? In this post, I explore that apparent paradox from the perspective of a central banker (though I remain a budget-conscious consumer when off duty).

title: AI Adoption and Employment Expectations: Evidence from a Survey of Small Business Owners
raw_summary: There is little consensus on the effect of AI adoption on employment. Economy-wide measures of pay and headcount have moved little even as AI adoption has spread rapidly, yet narrower measures document declining hiring for workers at the start of their careers or in AI-exposed occupations . In this post, we revisit this topic for U.S. small businesses. We use data from the 2025 Small Business Credit Survey (SBCS) to examine the twelve-month-forward employment and revenue expectations of AI users. We find that firms currently using AI are significantly more likely than non-users to expect increased employment and revenues over the next year, even after accounting for firm and owner characteristics and location. Revenue expectations are most optimistic for AI users that report facing operational challenges in utilizing technology.

title: Firm Heterogeneity and the Response of Investment to Monetary Policy
raw_summary: It is well known that monetary policy affects firms’ investment decisions. But which firms are the most responsive to changes in interest rates? And does this responsiveness vary over time? The literature has given diverse answers to this question, focusing on characteristics such as firm size, age, and financial position, and mostly studying these traits in isolation. In this post based on a recent Staff Report , we explore how investment responsiveness to monetary policy changes across firms and over time. We find that investment by most firms in most time periods responds little to monetary policy. For some firms in some periods, however, investment is very responsive to changes in interest rates. While these instances of strong sensitivity correlate with several firm traits, there is substantial variation that cannot easily be linked to specific characteristics of firms. Our findings therefore underscore the importance of considering the entire distribution of investment responses rather than focusing on the average effect.

title: How Fast Do Tariffs Pass Through into Consumer Prices?
raw_summary: There has been a lot of interest in how tariffs affect consumer prices (for example, Cavallo et al. 2021 , 2025 ). In this post, we present results from our new research paper that estimates the effects of the 2025-26 tariffs on retail consumer prices. We find that for every percentage point increase in average tariffs, consumer goods prices increase by about a quarter of a percent after one year. Roughly two-thirds of the effect arises because tariffs raise the prices of imported consumer goods. The remaining third arises indirectly: tariffs increase the prices of goods made in the U.S. because producers pay more for imported parts and materials, and because producers raise their markups when competing imports cost more. The effects differ in their timing. Prices of imported goods respond quickly to tariffs, while prices of U.S.-made goods adjust over six to twelve months as higher costs move through the supply chain.

title: Insured, but Still on the Hook: Who Bears the Most Risk in Homeowner’s Insurance?
raw_summary: In an April post , using millions of homeowners' insurance contracts matched with property-level exposure and disaster risk, we showed that although households are insured, they are still "on the hook” because deductibles and coverage limits leave homeowners responsible for part of a loss. Because insurers cannot perfectly observe how well homeowners maintain or protect their properties (a problem known as “moral hazard”), contract terms such as deductibles can play an important role in balancing risk sharing and incentives. By requiring homeowners to bear part of a loss, insurers can preserve incentives for policyholders to take actions that reduce damage risk. In this post, we quantify the cost of keeping homeowners on the hook. How costly is moral hazard in homeowner's insurance? How much risk must households retain to preserve these incentives? And, importantly, who ultimately bears that residual risk? The short answer is that keeping homeowners on the hook costs insurers relatively little, but it leaves households with substantial risk, especially those least able to absorb a large loss.

title: FEDS Paper: A Macroeconomic Analysis of Household Labor Supply Responses to Large Fiscal Transfers
raw_summary: Isabel Cairó , Shigeru Fujita, and Camilo Morales-Jimenez The fiscal transfers deployed during the COVID-19 pandemic were unprecedented in scale and strongly progressive. Using CPS/ASEC data, we document that the decline in employment during the pandemic was larger for low-income households and tightly linked to the intensity of transfer receipt, a pattern absent during the Global Financial Crisis. We develop and estimate a two-sector, heterogeneous-household general equilibrium model in which low-income households are borrowing-constrained in normal times but can save out of sufficiently large transfers. Because preferences permit wealth effects on labor supply, transfers both reduce labor supply and raise consumption, and a dollar of transfers is split roughly evenly between the two margins. We find that the effects of transfers are state-dependent: because the borrowing constraint binds more tightly in a deeper recession, the same transfer relaxes a tighter constraint and delivers an employment and consumption response about 40 to 50 percent larger during the pandemic than when the same transfer is introduced in the steady state. In the model, transfers were welfare-improving for recipients, with gains diminishing as transfers increase.

title: FEDS Paper: Inattentive Price Setting and Inflation Under Fiscal Policy Uncertainty
raw_summary: Oliver Pfäuti and Edson Wu How do high public debt and fiscal uncertainty interact to shape inflation? We develop a model in which firms face uncertainty about both marginal costs and fiscal policy and choose how much information to acquire before setting prices. Higher debt raises steady-state taxes, affecting attention through two opposing forces. While these taxes reduce the profit stakes of mispricing, they make desired prices more sensitive to tax fluctuations, increasing the value of information. The interaction generates a U-shaped relationship between public debt and attention, and therefore between debt and inflation volatility. Using euro-area firm-level expectations data, we document that the passthrough of expected input-cost growth into expected selling-price growth rises systematically with a country's debt-to-GDP ratio, consistent with the model. In the calibrated general-equilibrium model, an increase in debt from 100% to 175% of GDP raises inflation volatility by about 20%, mainly because firms reallocate attention toward fiscal shocks.

title: Operational excellence in serverless — 5E’s framework
raw_summary: Transform serverless freedom into business agility through the 5E’s framework: empower, engineer, evaluate, evolve and enhance. Modern digital businesses need software systems that are agile, reliable and cost-efficient. At Capital One, we’ve adopted a serverless-first approach to transform how we build and deploy applications, trading server management for a focus on delivering business value. While this paradigm eliminates operational overhead related to infrastructure, it doesn’t eliminate the need for operational excellence. In fact, the distributed, event-driven nature of serverless systems introduces a new set of challenges. When looking to achieve operational excellence in serverless systems, organizations must require disciplined engineering-automation, observability, cost control and a culture of continuous improvement. Understanding operational excellence in the serverless context Operational excellence focuses on how cloud systems are designed, deployed, monitored and optimized for long-term performance and reliability. In a serverless context, it involves: Automation : infrastructure and deployment as code Resilience : designing for failures, timeouts and throttling from day one Observability : collecting logs, metrics and traces across functions and services Cost visibility : paying only for what’s used, while avoiding hidden inefficiencies Continuous improvement : using data and feedback to refine architecture Serverless architecture can reduce reliance on infrastructure management, but it necessitates robust operational discipline to effectively handle distributed workloads. We will now delve into the five guiding principles, known as the 5E’s, which bridge the gap between operational excellence and practical engineering practices. Figure 1: Operational excellence illustrative architecture — The 5E’s Framework for Resilience & Agility Empower: automation and governance Empowerment starts with automation and clarity. Teams must have the freedom to deploy quickly while maintaining consistent operational standards. Engineering practices In practice, this balance is achieved through a core set of engineering practices: Infrastructure as code (IaC) : Use tools such as Terraform, Bicep or CloudFormation to version and review infrastructure changes. Continuous integration/continuous delivery (CI/CD) : Automate builds, tests and rollouts. Integrate static analysis and policy checks early. Policy as code : Apply guardrails for compliance and security directly in pipelines. Self-service deployment : Encourage “You build it, you run it” ownership with automated rollbacks and clear operational visibility. When developers are empowered through automation and safe defaults, organizations gain velocity without sacrificing control. Engineer: reliability, scalability and observability Engineering excellence is the foundation of operational maturity. In serverless environments, systems must be resilient, observable and scalable by design. Reliability patterns These patterns help serverless systems recover gracefully when things inevitably go wrong: Design idempotent functions to handle retries gracefully. Implement dead-letter queues (DLQs) for unprocessed events. Use managed workflow orchestration (e.g., Step Functions, Durable Functions or Workflows) to manage dependencies. Practice fault injection or chaos testing to validate recovery strategies. Scalability and performance These practices keep serverless systems fast and elastic as demand fluctuates: Adopt asynchronous eventing to decouple workloads. Use caching and edge delivery for latency-sensitive paths. Profile cold-start latency and optimize initialization logic. Observability These practices ensure teams can trace, measure and troubleshoot behavior across every function: Collect metrics, logs and traces across all functions. Correlate requests using trace IDs for end-to-end visibility. Build dashboards for throughput, errors and cost per invocation. By engineering observability and reliability into every function, teams can turn runtime behavior into actionable insights. Evaluate: measure what matters Operational excellence is measurable. Success should be based on objective signals, not assumptions. Here are some of the many metrics one might track: These dashboards are made visible within our engineering organization to create shared ownership. When teams track performance and cost together, they discover insights that help them balance agility and efficiency. Evolve: continuous optimization No architecture is ever “done.” Workloads, dependencies and customer expectations evolve, and your systems must evolve with them. Technical optimizations These optimizations keep infrastructure aligned with how the system actually runs, not how it was originally designed: Review usage patterns to tune memory, time-outs and concurrency. Migrate synchronous flows to event-driven designs for elasticity. Automate patching and runtime upgrades through IaC pipelines. Refactor high-cost or underperforming functions using data from cost and performance reports. Process evolution We cultivate an environment where reflection and adjustment happen as routinely as deployment: Schedule quarterly operational reviews focused on metrics, not just code. Introduce internal “learning sprints” where teams analyze incidents and share optimizations. Operational excellence thrives when teams treat every deployment as an opportunity to learn and refine. Enhance: feedback and learning loops The final step is enhancement, turning data into continuous improvement. Operational excellence isn’t static; it’s sustained through learning loops that connect incidents, telemetry and process improvements. Best practices Closing the loop between incidents and improvement comes down to a few key best practices: Conduct blameless postmortems after incidents and feed actions back into code or pipeline rules. Automate alerts for anomaly detection and integrate them with collaboration tools. Align retrospectives around measurable operational KPIs, not just delivery velocity. Reinforce psychological safety. Improvement happens when teams feel safe to surface failures early. Enhancement ensures that excellence becomes a habit, not a one-time achievement. Points to remember Pulling these ideas together, a few key takeaways stand out: Culture and empowerment : Great architecture stems from an empowered team, not just tools. By automating routine workflows, we empower developers to focus on higher-level problem-solving, reinforcing that automation is a partner to human ingenuity, not a replacement. Metrics and customer impact : Use metrics like latency, reliability and cost to gain clarity, always linking them back to how they affect the customer. Visibility and trust: Foster trust by making operational data accessible to everyone. Automation and innovation : Automation frees up time from manual tasks, allowing for greater innovation and improvement. Continuous learning and reliability : Sustain reliability through ongoing evolution of architecture, processes and people. Conclusion Serverless technology frees engineers from infrastructure, but operational excellence transforms that freedom into business agility. It’s not just about scaling code; it’s about scaling learning. By empowering teams with automation, engineering for resilience, evaluating what matters, evolving with data and enhancing through feedback, we’re building cloud systems that are reliable, efficient and continually improving. Operational excellence isn’t a destination-it’s the rhythm of modern serverless architecture. Originally published at https://www.capitalone.com .
